# Write PR Descriptions

Write PRs that a teammate can understand at a glance. Lead with what was broken from the user's point of view, then show the fix in plain words with a concrete before/after. No padding, no checkbox theater, no jargon-first openings.

This is the default quality bar from the first draft. Don't ship a generic version expecting to fix it after feedback.

## 0. The prefilled template

GitHub prefills every PR from `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, which asks for Summary, Testing, Demo, Checklist, and Contributor Resources. That is not what this repo's PRs look like. Replace the prefilled body with the structure in section 2.

Two parts of the template still apply:

- **Demo.** UI changes need a capture from the real app running your branch. Never substitute a mock-up, a component harness, or a recreated screen. If you cannot run the app, say the demo is outstanding and why, rather than filling the space with something that proves nothing.
- **Testing.** Keep the substance under a `## Tests` heading. You do not need the template's three subheadings unless the change is large enough that they help.

Drop the Checklist and Contributor Resources if the author is a core maintainer of the repo. They exist for first-time outside contributors and the team does not fill them in.

## 1. Title

The title states the actual change in plain words.

- Use the conventional prefix the repo already uses, e.g. `[fix] <Title>`, `[feat] <Title>`, `[chore] <Title>`, `[docs] <Title>`.
- If the user gave you an issue id, suffix it: `[fix] <Title> [AGE-1234]`.
- Define the title as an active intent in present tense, e.g `[fix] Resolve broken evaluation links`.
- Keep it under ~70 characters. Detail goes in the body.

Good vs bad:

- Good: `[fix] Map OpenInference tool definitions into real tool objects`
- Bad: `fix(api) parse X into structured objects` (abstract, says nothing concrete)
- Bad: `Update tool handling` (vague, no symptom, no domain)

## 2. Body structure

Use this shape unless the change is truly trivial:

```
## Context
<one or two sentences: the symptom a user or teammate would notice, then the root cause in plain words>

## Changes
<plain-words explanation of the change, with a concrete before/after when a data shape, signature, or behavior changed>

## Tests / notes
<short bullet list or prose: what you verified, anything reviewers should watch for>

## What to QA
<only for user-visible changes: short steps for the manual tester, see section 7>
```

Adapt the headings if the situation calls for it (e.g. a pure feature PR might use "What this adds" instead of "What was broken"). The order stays the same: the obeservation (symptom or user-visible change first or intent), then the changes, then verification and validation.

## 3. Show, don't restate the diff

When a transformation changed a data shape, signature, or behavior, show it concretely.

Good:

> Tool definitions coming from OpenInference traces arrived as
>
> ```
> [{tool: {json_schema: "..."}}]
> ```
>
> The playground expected
>
> ```
> [{type: "function", function: {...}}]
> ```
>
> So the parser now unwraps `json_schema` and rebuilds each entry in the expected shape before handing it to the playground.

Bad:

> - Updated tool parsing logic
> - Improved data handling
> - Added support for OpenInference tools

The second version restates the diff in vague bullets. It tells the reader nothing the file list doesn't.

## 4. Cut the padding

Things to remove before you publish:

- Generic "Summary" or "Overview" sections that paraphrase the title.
- Checkbox theater ("- [x] code written - [x] tested") unless the repo's template requires it.
- Bullet lists that restate every changed file. The diff already shows that.
- Marketing words: "comprehensive", "robust", "seamlessly", "leverage", "powerful".
- Bullets that exist only to fill space. Prefer one clear sentence to three vague bullets.

## 5. Prose rules

Apply these general writing rules:

- **No em dashes.** Replace with a period and a new sentence, parentheses, or a semicolon. Absolute rule.
- Active voice.
- Short sentences by default. Longer ones only when they help the flow.
- Complete sentences. Snippets are fine when they keep things short and clear.
- Don't overuse bold or bullets. Use them when they aid quick reading. Otherwise prose.
- 11th-grade English, except for unavoidable technical terms.

## 6. Tests / notes section

Keep this section short and concrete. Useful contents:

- What you ran locally (`pnpm test`, `pytest tests/...`, manual UI check on `/observability`).
- Anything reviewers should poke at (a known-fragile area, a follow-up not in this PR).
- Migration or rollout notes if relevant.

Skip the section entirely if there is nothing real to say. A blank "Tests" heading is worse than no heading.

## 7. What to QA section

If the change is user-visible and a teammate will test it manually, add a "What to QA" section. Write it for a tester who knows the product and has context: skip the basics, point at the right screens, and state the expected result of every check.

- One line per check: where to go, what to do, what they should see.
- Name the exact pages and flows. "Test the feature" is not a check.
- Include the regression to watch for: the thing this change is most likely to have broken.
- If a check needs setup (a seeded project, an older record, a feature flag), say so in the same line.
- Use simple, clear language. Same prose rules as section 5.

Example:

> ## What to QA
> - Create a new automatic evaluator, name it, save. The table shows your name with a v1 tag, not "default".
> - Edit it and commit a config change. The name stays, the version bumps to v2.
> - Regression: run a new evaluation. The variant chips still say "default", not the app name.

Skip the section when nothing is user-visible (pure refactor, CI, docs). A reviewer-only change needs the Tests section, not this one.

## 8. Reviewer's first-30-seconds test

Before you finalize, read your own draft and ask:

1. After 30 seconds, does a reviewer know **the context** and **what changed**?
2. Is there a concrete before/after anywhere a shape or behavior moved?
3. Did you delete every sentence that doesn't earn its place?
4. Did you scan for em dashes and marketing words?

If any answer is no, edit before you push.

## 9. Worked example

A bad first draft:

```
## Summary
- Updated the tool parsing logic to handle OpenInference traces
- Improved compatibility with the playground
- Added robust error handling for edge cases

## Includes
- Modified parseTools function
- Updated type definitions
- Added new test cases
```

A good rewrite:

```
## Context
When you opened an OpenInference trace in the playground, the tools panel was empty. The trace stored tool definitions as `[{tool: {json_schema: "..."}}]`, but the playground expected the OpenAI shape `[{type: "function", function: {...}}]`, so the parser dropped them silently.

## Changes
`parseToolsFromTrace` now unwraps `json_schema` and rebuilds each entry in the OpenAI shape before it hits the playground. Traces that already use the OpenAI shape pass through unchanged.

Before:
[{tool: {json_schema: "{\"name\": \"get_weather\", ...}"}}]

After:
[{type: "function", function: {name: "get_weather", parameters: {...}}}]

## Tests
- Added a unit test in parseToolsFromTrace.test.ts covering both shapes.
- Opened a real OpenInference trace from the staging project and confirmed the tools panel renders.

## What to QA
- Open an OpenInference trace in the playground (the staging project has them). The tools panel lists the tools.
- Regression: open a trace from the OpenAI SDK. The tools panel still renders as before.
```

The second version is cleaner and tells the reviewer everything they need to start reading the diff.

## Context

A user who makes an event automation ("when a pull request opens in GitHub, review it") cannot see or use what is in the event. The Instruction box on `/m` is a plain text box, so the stored instruction is static text. The agent never gets the pull request, the email or the message that started the run. The old field picker was deleted with the old subscription form in `89c2d80c39`.

The backend PR under this one (#7911) adds the full event to the agent's message by default (`data.include_event`) and records the event on each delivery (`data.event`). This PR is the screen for it.

## Changes

For event automations only, the Instruction field now has four parts. Schedules keep today's plain composer.

1. **Pills in the instruction.** The text box is a small rich editor. An event field shows as a chip (a "pill") with its label and an x. Backspace or the x removes it like one character.
2. **Field cards.** Under the box, one card per field of the event's payload schema, which the catalog already returns from Composio. Each card shows a humanized name (`createdBy` reads "Created by") and Composio's own description. A click adds the field as a pill. A card whose field is already in the instruction shows a check.
3. **Include-event checkbox.** "Also attach the full event, so the agent can use any detail". It reads `data.include_event`. An automation saved before this change has no key, so it reads as checked.
4. **"What the agent gets" preview.** The exact text the agent gets. Pills take their values from the newest delivery that recorded an event. With no such delivery, each pill shows as its label in square brackets, for example `[Title]`.

**How a pill is stored.** A pill is a text part whose text is a selector into the event: `$.event.attributes.<key>`. The dispatcher already replaces a selector with its value. For "Review " and the Title pill, the stored mapping is:

```json
{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": [
  {"type": "text", "text": "Review "},
  {"type": "text", "text": "$.event.attributes.title"}
]}]}
```

A key with characters other than letters, digits and underscores uses the bracket form, `$.event.attributes["a.b"]`. A pill is always a text part, even when it is alone, so a field that holds a list stays text.

**Run now** sends the preview text. When the user presses it, the screen fetches the deliveries once, takes the newest recorded event, and builds the text with the same function the preview uses. If that fetch fails, no run starts, the error goes to the console, and the button stays usable. A mapping the composer cannot show (several messages, a non-user message) keeps today's warning and today's Run now text.

**Other mapping keys are kept.** Reading and writing the instruction now changes only the message key. Before, a builder agent's mapping with a sibling key (for example `"event": "$.event.attributes"`) showed as an empty box, and a save dropped that key.

Where the code sits, mapped to backend layers:

- `@agenta/entities/gatewayTrigger/core` is the pure-function layer, like a `core` module with pytest tests: the schema-to-cards rules, the template read and write, the preview text, and the newest-event pick. The event text format and the value rule (a string unchanged, null empty, anything else compact JSON) mirror the Python ones and are pinned by the same fixtures.
- `@agenta/entity-ui` holds the two reusable components: `EventMessageComposer` (over a restored `PillEditor`) and `EventFieldCards`.
- `@agenta/automation-ui` wires them into the Instruction field and adds `includeEvent` to the unsaved form state of the create and detail screens (the "draft", like a request body built field by field until Save).
- `web/mobile` changes the Run now button and menu item.

The Fern client types for `TriggerSubscriptionData` and `TriggerDeliveryData` are regenerated from the EE OpenAPI spec of a stack that runs the backend branch. The run also changed two unrelated generated files (a docstring from another endpoint and the default server URL); they are left out.

## Scope and risk

- Event automations on `/m` only. The classic app under `/w` is not touched.
- An old automation opens with the checkbox checked, because the backend reads a missing key as on. Saving it writes `include_event: true` explicitly.
- Typed text that starts with `$` or `/` is still read as a selector by the backend. This is a known limit and is not changed here.

## Tests

- `@agenta/entities` unit tests (vitest): 186 files, 2638 tests pass. New tests cover the seven GitHub pull request cards and labels, a nested Linear-style group, bracket selectors and a quoted key with a dot, sibling keys kept on write, a pill moved from a completion shape to a chat shape, the newest event from unsorted rows, the preview with and without an event, the value fixtures (string, number, boolean, object, array, absent), and the shared event text example.
- `web/mobile` unit tests: 120 files, 720 tests pass, including a new test for the Run now text (with a delivery, with none, with a failed call, and with a mapping the composer cannot show).
- Type checks pass for `@agenta/entities`, `@agenta/entity-ui`, `@agenta/automation-ui` and `web/mobile`. `pnpm lint-fix` is clean. Storybook lints and builds, with a new `EventMessageComposer` story.
- Live check on a local EE stack running both branches, in `/m`, as a new account:
  - Detail screen of an automation saved before this change: the checkbox is checked. Unchecking shows the save bar and Discard checks it again. Uncheck, Save, reload: still unchecked.
  - Typing text and clicking "Title" adds a pill and checks the card. The stored mapping has the `$.event.attributes.title` part. Backspace and the x both remove the pill.
  - After one signed GitHub pull request event, the preview shows the real title in place of the pill and the event block. The text matches what the dispatcher sent, except for the key order inside the event JSON (Postgres stores the event as `jsonb`, which reorders keys).
  - At 390 px the cards are one column and the page does not scroll sideways.
- Not checked live: Run now and the create step. The local stack has no real GitHub connection and the test agent did not appear in the agent picker, so neither could start. The session workspace drawer was not opened; it renders the same component.

## What to QA

- Open an event automation (GitHub pull request event) on `/m`. Under the Instruction box, cards show with Composio's descriptions. Click "Title": a pill appears and the card shows a check.
- The checkbox reads "Also attach the full event, so the agent can use any detail" and is checked on an automation made before this release. Uncheck, Save, reload: unchecked. Discard before Save brings it back.
- Make a pull request in the connected repo. Reopen the automation: the preview shows the real title and the event JSON. Run now opens a chat whose first message has the same text.
- Create a new event automation with a pill and save it. The run that follows gets the title in the message.
- Regression: a schedule automation still shows the plain Instruction box with "Sent to the agent on every run."
